answers.question: List of scenarios
answers.answer: Three scenarios were used: 1) Net Zero 2050 (Orderly Category) — aligned with IPCC SSP1-1.9/RCP1.9 and NZ CCC "Tailwinds"; 2) Delayed Transition (Disorderly Category) — aligned with IPCC SSP1-2.6/RCP2.6 and NZ CCC "Headwinds"; 3) Current Policies (Hot House World Category) — aligned with IPCC SSP3-7.0/RCP7.0 and NZ CCC "Current Policy Reference".
answers.evidence: "Net Zero 2050 (Orderly Category) | Delayed Transition (Disorderly Category) | Current Policies (Hot House World Category) ... Shared socio-economic Pathway (SSP)-Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) SSP1-1.9/RCP1.9 | SSP1-2.6/RCP2.6 | SSP3-7.0/RCP7.0 ... Tailwinds | Headwinds | Current Policy Reference"
answers.notes: These scenarios were co-designed with other NZ retailers and KPMG New Zealand and published in a report entitled "The Futures of Retail".

answers.question: Global temperature outcome by 2100
answers.answer:
The document describes three scenarios with the following global temperature outcomes by 2100:
1. Net Zero 2050 (Orderly): 1.4°C by 2100
2. Delayed Transition (Disorderly): 1.6°C by 2100
3. Current Policies (Hot House World): more than 3°C by 2100
answers.evidence: "limits global warming to 1.6°C in 2050 and reducing to 1.4°C by 2100" (Net Zero 2050); "limits global warming to 1.7°C in 2050 and reducing to 1.6°C by 2100" (Delayed Transition); "resulting in 2°C global warming by 2050 and more than 3°C by 2100" (Current Policies)
answers.notes: Three distinct scenarios are presented, each with explicit 2100 temperature outcomes.

answers.question: Scenario provider
answers.answer: Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), with scenarios co-designed in collaboration with KPMG New Zealand
answers.evidence: The sector group chose three Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios as the basis for the sector-level scenarios... In 2023, we collaborated with other New Zealand retailers that are climate reporting entities and KPMG New Zealand to co-design a set of integrated climate change scenarios for New Zealand's retail sector.
answers.notes: The NGFS scenarios were used as the basis, while KPMG New Zealand facilitated the co-design process for the retail sector-specific scenarios. IPCC and New Zealand Climate Change Commission (CCC) scenarios were also referenced as additional frameworks.

answers.question: Pick-and-mix of SSPs and RCPs
answers.answer:
Briscoe Group uses the following SSP-RCP combinations across its three scenarios:
1. Net Zero 2050 (Orderly): SSP1-1.9 / RCP1.9
2. Delayed Transition (Disorderly): SSP1-2.6 / RCP2.6
3. Current Policies (Hot House World): SSP3-7.0 / RCP7.0
answers.evidence: "Shared socio-economic Pathway (SSP)-Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) SSP1-1.9/RCP1.9 [Net Zero 2050] | SSP1-2.6/RCP2.6 [Delayed Transition] | SSP3-7.0/RCP7.0 [Current Policies]"
answers.notes: Each scenario maps to a distinct SSP-RCP pairing. The Net Zero 2050 scenario uses SSP1-1.9/RCP1.9, the Delayed Transition uses SSP1-2.6/RCP2.6, and the Current Policies (Hot House World) uses SSP3-7.0/RCP7.0.

answers.question: Customised scenarios
answers.answer: Briscoe Group did not develop fully customised scenarios. Instead, they used sector-level scenarios developed by a retail sector working group, based on three NGFS scenarios: Orderly (Net Zero 2025), Disorderly (Delayed Transition), and Hot House World (Current Policies). These were adapted into retail sector narratives across three time horizons (short: 2023–2030, medium: 2031–2040, long: 2041–2050).
answers.evidence: The sector group chose three Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios as the basis for the sector-level scenarios. These were: Orderly Category: Net Zero 2025, Disorderly Category: Delayed Transition and Hot House World Category: Current Policies. A retail sector narrative was formed for each scenario identifying the critical interactions and key outcomes and indicators. These scenarios considered three different time horizons: short (2023-2030), medium (2031-2040) and long (2041-2050) and explored the political, environmental, societal, technological, legal and economic impacts across each potential pathway.
answers.notes: The scenarios were sector-level adaptations of NGFS scenarios, not fully bespoke/customised scenarios developed independently by Briscoe Group.

answers.question: Co-produced climate scenarios
answers.answer: Yes. In 2023, Briscoe Group collaborated with other New Zealand retailers that are climate reporting entities and KPMG New Zealand to co-design a set of integrated climate change scenarios for New Zealand's retail sector. These scenarios are detailed in a published report entitled "The Futures of Retail" published on the KPMG website, and included the development of three climate scenarios.

answers.question: Baseline scenarios
answers.answer: The baseline scenario represents 1.1°C of global warming, used to identify current physical and transition impacts. Two further scenarios were also used: 1.5°C and 3.0°C of global warming. These correspond to: Net Zero 2050 (Orderly Category, IPCC SSP1-1.9/RCP1.9, NZ CCC "Tailwinds"), Delayed Transition (Disorderly Category, IPCC SSP1-2.6/RCP2.6 and SSP3-7.0/RCP7.0, NZ CCC "Headwinds"), and Current Policies / Hot House World (IPCC SSP3-7.0/RCP7.0, NZ CCC "Current Policy Reference").
answers.evidence: "A baseline risk assessment representing 1.1°C of global warming helping us to identify the current physical and transition impacts we have incurred. Two further scenarios representing 1.5°C and 3.0°C of global warming."
answers.notes: The baseline is 1.1°C. The three scenario categories (Orderly, Disorderly, Hot House) are detailed on page 32 with their IPCC and NZ CCC equivalents.

answers.question: Model used
answers.answer: No modelling was undertaken. The scenario analysis was performed as a stand-alone process without any modelling integrated into usual strategy processes.
answers.evidence: "The first iteration of our Scenario analysis, climate-risk assessment, and transition planning has been performed as a stand-alone process, no modelling was undertaken, and it was not integrated into our usual strategy processes."
answers.location_hint: Briscoe Group 2025 Annual Report, Climate-Related Disclosures, p.32
answers.notes: The scenarios used were co-designed with KPMG New Zealand and other NZ retailers, referencing IPCC SSP/RCP pathways and NZ Climate Change Commission scenarios, but no quantitative modelling tool or model name is mentioned.

answers.question: Damage from acute physical risk considered
answers.answer: Yes. Briscoe Group considers damage from acute physical risks including: increased storminess/extreme winds, river and pluvial flooding, sea-level rise leading to coastal and estuarine flooding, and supply chain disruptions from storms/floods affecting ports and highways. Potential financial impacts include cost of repairs/maintenance to buildings, increased lease costs, increased supply chain costs, increased insurance premiums, and loss of sales/decrease in profit.
answers.evidence:
"Increase in storminess (frequency, intensity) including tropical cyclones. Changes in extreme wind speed. Increase in convective weather events (tornadoes, lightning). Changes in extremes: high intensity and persistence of rainfall. Increase in hail severity or frequency... Loss of sales and decrease in profit. Cost of repairs/maintenance to buildings. Increased lease costs. Increased supply chain costs. Increased insurance premiums."

"Sea level rise of 0.32m could impact specific locations and increase losses due to flooding. Temporary store closures. Delays in supply chain... Cost of repairs/maintenance to buildings. Increased lease costs. Increased supply chain costs."

"A main international port is affected (e.g. by storms/or floods). New Zealand shipping port or main highway is affected (e.g. by storms/or floods). Unable to get goods to New Zealand... Loss of sales and decrease in profit. Increased supply chain costs."
answers.notes: The document explicitly identifies multiple acute physical risks (storms, flooding, sea-level rise, supply chain disruptions) and their associated financial impacts, along with building block actions to address them.

answers.question: Scale of scenarios
answers.answer: Briscoe Group used three scenarios representing different scales of global warming: a baseline of 1.1°C, and two further scenarios of 1.5°C and 3.0°C of global warming. These correspond to: (1) Net Zero 2050 / Orderly (SSP1-1.9/RCP1.9, SSP1-2.6/RCP2.6) — limiting warming to 1.6°C in 2050, reducing to 1.4°C by 2100; (2) Delayed Transition / Disorderly (SSP3-7.0/RCP7.0) — limiting warming to 1.7°C in 2050, reducing to 1.6°C by 2100; and (3) Current Policies / Hothouse World — resulting in 2°C by 2050 and more than 3°C by 2100.
answers.evidence: "A baseline risk assessment representing 1.1°C of global warming helping us to identify the current physical and transition impacts we have incurred. Two further scenarios representing 1.5°C and 3.0°C of global warming."
answers.notes: The three scenarios are clearly described with their temperature scales and corresponding IPCC/NZ CCC scenario labels on pages 31–32.

answers.question: Justification for scenario/model choice
answers.answer: Briscoe Group chose three NGFS-based scenarios (Net Zero 2025, Delayed Transition, and Current Policies) co-designed with other New Zealand retailers and KPMG New Zealand as part of a retail sector scenario project ("The Futures of Retail"). The justification for using a combination of scenarios was to add resilience to the risk assessment process and the resultant strategy in preparation for inevitable uncertainty in the short to medium-term. The scenarios covered three warming levels (1.1°C baseline, 1.5°C, and 3.0°C) and three time horizons (short, medium, long), allowing the company to assess both physical and transition risks across different pathways.
answers.evidence: "The sector group chose three Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios as the basis for the sector-level scenarios. These were: Orderly Category: Net Zero 2025, Disorderly Category: Delayed Transition and Hot House World Category: Current Policies... Using a combination of scenarios was intended to add resilience to the risk assessment process and the resultant strategy as we prepare for inevitable uncertainty in the short to medium-term."
answers.notes: The scenarios were developed collaboratively with other NZ retailers and KPMG NZ in 2023, published as "The Futures of Retail." No quantitative modelling was undertaken; the process was qualitative and workshop-based.

answers.question: Direct and indirect physical climate risks
answers.answer:
Briscoe Group identifies the following key physical climate risks:

1. **Sustainable Sourcing (indirect):** Climate-related events increasing globally pose a significant risk to the availability and consistent supply of raw materials used by suppliers to manufacture products, potentially decreasing inventory availability, increasing costs, and decreasing margins/profit.

2. **Increased storminess / extreme winds / river and pluvial flooding (direct & indirect):** Increase in storminess (frequency, intensity) including tropical cyclones, changes in extreme wind speed, convective weather events, high-intensity rainfall, and hail severity/frequency. Impacts include potential store closures, delays in supply chain, staff and customers unable to reach stores, loss of sales, cost of repairs/maintenance, increased lease costs, increased supply chain costs, and increased insurance premiums.

3. **Sea-level rise leading to coastal and estuarine flooding (direct):** Also identified as a physical risk (details partially cut off in context).

These risks were assessed across short (1–3 years), medium (>3–10 years), and long-term (>10 years) horizons under 1.5°C and 3.0°C warming scenarios, with physical impacts being most severe under the 3.0°C Hothouse World scenario.
answers.evidence: "KEY PHYSICAL RISKS: Sustainable Sourcing — With climate-related events increasing globally, there is a significant risk to the availability and consistent supply of raw materials used by our suppliers to manufacture products... Increased storminess/extreme winds, River and pluvial flooding — Increase in storminess (frequency, intensity) including tropical cyclones. Changes in extreme wind speed. Increase in convective weather events (tornadoes, lightning). Changes in extremes: high intensity and persistence of rainfall. Increase in hail severity or frequency... There will be an increasing incidence of storm events with increasing severity impacting supply chains and operations. Potential store closures. Delays in supply chain. Staff and customers unable to get to our stores. Loss of sales and decrease in profit. Cost of repairs/maintenance to buildings. Increased lease costs. Increased supply chain costs. Increased insurance premiums... Sea-level rise leading to coastal and estuarine flooding."
answers.notes: The sea-level rise risk entry is cut off in the retrieved context, so full details of its impacts and mitigations are not available. The sustainable sourcing risk is indirect (supply chain), while storminess/flooding risks are both direct (operations/stores) and indirect (supply chain).
